chapter.name: Fractions
chapter.blurb: Fractional units and equal shares, reading and naming fractions, marking fractions on a number line, mixed numbers, equivalent fractions and lowest terms, comparing fractions, and adding/subtracting fractions using Brahmagupta's method.

scope_in.item: Read a fraction as an equal share of a whole and identify the fractional unit obtained when 1 whole is divided into n equal parts (e.g., 1/2, 1/4, 1/9)
Compare unit fractions directly using the rule that sharing the same whole among more people gives a smaller share (e.g. 1/9 < 1/5)
Identify the fractional unit represented by one piece of a whole cut into equal parts, and build a general fraction as a given number of fractional units (e.g. 3/4 as '3 times 1/4')
Name the numerator and denominator of a fraction
Mark and read the length of a fraction on a number line, including recognising that infinitely many fractions lie between 0 and 1
Tell whether a fraction is less than or greater than 1 by comparing its numerator and denominator
Find the number of whole units in a fraction greater than 1 and write it as a mixed number; convert a mixed number back to a single fraction
Generate equivalent fractions of a given fraction using a fraction wall, paper folding, or by multiplying/dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number
Express a fraction in its lowest terms (simplest form) by dividing numerator and denominator by their highest common factor, in one step or in stages
Compare two or more fractions by converting them to equivalent fractions with a common denominator and comparing numerators; write fractions in ascending or descending order
Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator by adding or subtracting numerators and keeping the denominator unchanged
Add and subtract fractions with different denominators using Brahmagupta's method: find a common denominator, add/subtract the numerators, then simplify to lowest terms if needed
Solve word problems on lengths, volumes and time that require adding or subtracting fractions

concepts.name: Unit fractions as equal shares
concepts.description: Fractions arising from sharing 1 whole equally among some number of people, and comparing such unit fractions.
concepts.idea: A unit fraction is what one share becomes when a whole is split equally among a number of people; splitting among more people always makes each share smaller.
concepts.rule: When 1 whole is shared equally among n people, each share is the fractional unit 1/n; if n1 > n2 then 1/n1 < 1/n2.
concepts.example: 1 roti shared among 2 children gives 1/2 each; shared among 9 children gives 1/9 each, and 1/9 < 1/2.

concepts.name: Fractional units as parts of a whole, and reading fractions
concepts.description: Building a general fraction from a number of fractional units, and naming the numerator and denominator.
concepts.idea: A whole divided into equal parts gives fractional units; collecting m of them gives the general fraction m/n, read as 'm times 1/n'.
concepts.rule: In the fraction a/b, a is the numerator (how many fractional units are taken) and b is the denominator (the number of equal parts the whole is divided into); a/b = a times (1/b).
concepts.example: A chikki cut into 4 equal pieces has fractional unit 1/4; taking 3 of those pieces gives 3/4, i.e. '3 times 1/4', where 3 is the numerator and 4 is the denominator.

concepts.name: Mixed fractions
concepts.description: Converting a fraction greater than 1 into a mixed number, and back into a single fraction.
concepts.idea: A fraction greater than 1 (numerator bigger than denominator) contains some whole units plus a leftover fractional part, which can be written together as a mixed number.
concepts.rule: To convert a/b (a > b) to a mixed number, find how many whole times b divides into a; the quotient is the whole part and the remainder over b is the fractional part. To convert back, multiply the whole part by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the same denominator.
concepts.example: 8/3 = 2 whole units and 2/3 left over, written as 2 2/3; conversely, 2 2/3 = (2x3+2)/3 = 8/3.

concepts.name: Equivalent fractions and lowest terms
concepts.description: Recognising and generating equivalent fractions, and reducing a fraction to its simplest form.
concepts.idea: Two fractions are equivalent when they represent the same share or the same point on the number line, even though they use different fractional units.
concepts.rule: Multiplying (or dividing) both the numerator and denominator of a fraction by the same non-zero number gives an equivalent fraction; a fraction is in lowest terms when its numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1.
concepts.example: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8 are all equivalent; 16/20 divided by the common factor 4 gives the lowest terms 4/5.

concepts.name: Comparing fractions
concepts.description: Comparing and ordering fractions using a common denominator.
concepts.idea: Fractions with different denominators cannot be compared by looking at the numerators alone; they must first be rewritten with the same fractional unit.
concepts.rule: To compare fractions, convert them to equivalent fractions with a common denominator (e.g. the product of the denominators), then the fraction with the greater numerator is greater.
concepts.example: To compare 4/5 and 7/9, rewrite as 36/45 and 35/45; since 36 > 35, 4/5 > 7/9.

concepts.name: Addition and subtraction of fractions (Brahmagupta's method)
concepts.description: Adding and subtracting fractions with the same and with different denominators, using a common-denominator method.
concepts.idea: Fractions can only be added or subtracted directly when they share the same fractional unit; fractions with different denominators must first be converted to a common one.
concepts.rule: Brahmagupta's method: (1) find a common denominator for all the fractions, e.g. the product of the denominators or their smallest common multiple, (2) add or subtract the numerators of the resulting equivalent fractions, keeping the denominator unchanged, (3) reduce the answer to lowest terms if needed.
